topics: 👑 Ten Questions — Alexander of Macedon interrogates the Elders of the Negev
🗺️ Into the Mountains of Darkness — donkeys, ropes, and a city of women
👁️ The Eyeball at the Gate of Eden — a parable about a gaze that is never satisfied
📖 'Torah Scholars Increase Peace' — closing words on the value of nighttime study
🎲 Two More Lotteries — for the incense, and for carrying limbs up to the altar

overview.title: 📖 Overview: A King's Questions, and the Chapter's Close
overview.subtitle: Tamid 32a–32b
overview.label: The scene:
overview.text: Continuing from the previous daf's mention of sunlight and the altar, the Gemara records a lengthy exchange between Alexander of Macedon and the Elders of the Negev — ten probing questions about the cosmos, wisdom, wealth, and how to be accepted by others. The narrative follows Alexander on a fantastical journey through the Mountains of Darkness, an encounter with a city ruled entirely by women, and a visit to the very gate of the Garden of Eden, where a single eyeball outweighs all his treasure until covered with dust. The chapter then closes with teachings praising nighttime Torah study, before a new mishna resumes the Temple service: the priests' recitation of Shema and blessings, followed by two more lotteries — for burning the incense, and for carrying the limbs up to the altar.

slides.title: 👑 A Selection of Alexander's Questions
slides.subtitle: Wisdom the Elders of the Negev offered the Macedonian king
rows: 'The one who sees and anticipates the consequences of his behavior' (הָרוֹאֶה אֶת הַנּוֹלָד)
'The one who masters his own desire' (הַכּוֹבֵשׁ אֶת יִצְרוֹ)
'The one who is content with his own portion' (הַשָּׂמֵחַ בְּחֶלְקוֹ)
Is it better to live at sea or on dry land?
Dry land — sailors' minds are never truly settled until they reach shore
'We are all equal — every question you ask, we answer as one'

callout.label: A tense exchange:
callout.text: When Alexander threatened execution for their 'defiance,' the Elders replied that a king's power is real, but falsehood is unbecoming of a king who had pledged them no harm — and Alexander, impressed, honored them with royal garments and golden chains instead.

slides.title: 🗺️ Through the Mountains of Darkness
slides.subtitle: A journey ending at the gate of the Garden of Eden

steps.content: 1️⃣ Wanting to campaign in Africa, Alexander is advised to bring Libyan donkeys (suited to darkness) and coils of rope to mark his path through the Mountains of Darkness
2️⃣ He reaches a town ruled entirely by women, who decline battle (a loss either way would shame him) and instead serve him bread made of GOLD — teaching him he came not for food, but for wealth
3️⃣ Later, resting by a fragrant spring, he suspects it flows from the Garden of Eden and follows it to its gate, demanding entry
4️⃣ Denied entry as unrighteous, he asks for a gift instead and receives a single eyeball — which, when weighed, outweighs ALL his gold and silver combined

5️⃣ The Sages explain: it's a mortal eye, never satisfied while it can see — proven when covering it with a bit of dirt instantly balances the scale, per Proverbs 27:20: 'the eyes of man are never satiated'

slides.title: 📖 Closing the Chapter: The Value of Nighttime Torah Study
slides.subtitle: Praise for Torah scholars, marking the end of this section
slides.hebrewSource: וְכׇל בָּנַיִךְ לִמּוּדֵי ה׳ וְרַב שְׁלוֹם בָּנָיִךְ
slides.label: Two teachings:
slides.text: Rabbi Ḥiyya taught: anyone who occupies himself with Torah study at night is accompanied by the Divine Presence, drawing on Lamentations 2:19's call to 'arise, cry out in the night... pour out your heart before the Lord.' Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya added: Torah scholars increase peace in the world, reading Isaiah 54:13's 'your children (בָּנַיִךְ)' as 'your builders (בּוֹנַיִךְ)' — scholars literally build peace for the world through their study.

slides.title: 📖 New Mishna: Shema and Blessings
slides.subtitle: The priests' prayers after laying the offering on the ramp
rows: A single blessing from the Shema liturgy
The Ten Commandments, Shema, VeHaya Im Shamoa, and VaYomer
Emet VeYatziv (redemption), the Temple service blessing, and the Priestly Blessing (recited, not with hands raised)
An extra blessing added by the outgoing watch, wishing love and friendship upon the incoming one

slides.title: 🎲 The Third and Fourth Lotteries
slides.subtitle: Incense, limb-carrying, and preparing the incense-bearer

nodes.content: 🎲 Third lottery: only priests who had NEVER burned the incense before could participate — a lifetime honor given just once
🎲 Fourth lottery (new AND experienced priests together): who carries the limbs from the ramp's lower half up onto the altar itself

👕 Priests who didn't win any lottery — still dressed for potential service — were handed to attendants, who removed their sacred vestments (four labeled storage compartments: trousers, tunic, belt, mitre) down to their trousers alone
🥄 The incense winner took the ceremonial spoon (like a large gold vessel holding 3 kav) with a smaller vessel nestled inside it, ready to carry the incense to the golden altar

summary.principle: The chapter closes by pairing worldly wisdom — Alexander's philosophical exchange with the Elders of the Negev, culminating in the lesson that human desire is never fully satisfied — with the Temple's own disciplined rhythm of prayer and lottery, where even undressing after a lost lottery followed a precise, orderly protocol.

flowSteps.content: 👑 Alexander questions the Elders on wisdom, strength, wealth, and human nature
🗺️ His journey through the Mountains of Darkness leads to a lesson about wealth (the women's town) and desire (the eyeball at Eden's gate)
📖 The chapter closes praising nighttime Torah study as a source of peace and divine closeness

columns.content: 📖 New mishna: priests recite Shema and blessings before continuing the service
🎲 Two more lotteries determine who burns the incense and who carries limbs to the altar

flowSteps.content: 🎓 Key Principle: whether in worldly wisdom or Temple ritual, true value lies in restraint, contentment, and precise devotion — never in unchecked desire

quiz.q: According to the Elders of the Negev's answer to Alexander, who is considered truly wise?
o: The one who has the most books
The one who sees and anticipates the consequences of his behavior (הָרוֹאֶה אֶת הַנּוֹלָד)
The one who wins every argument
The one who has traveled the most
quiz.e: The Elders answer with the classic teaching that true wisdom lies in foreseeing the consequences of one's actions, a formulation also found in Pirkei Avot.

quiz.q: What happened when Alexander asked the women's town for bread and they served him bread made of gold?
o: He was pleased and stayed there
He questioned why they gave him inedible gold bread, and they responded that he must have really come for wealth, not food, since he had bread at home
He declared war immediately
He refused to eat anything they offered
quiz.e: The women's pointed response taught Alexander that his campaign was truly about seeking wealth, not sustenance, since he already had bread available at home.

quiz.q: What lesson did Alexander learn from the eyeball he received at the gate of the Garden of Eden?
o: That gold is more valuable than anything else
That a mortal eye is never satisfied while it can see — demonstrated when covering it with a small amount of dirt balanced the scale against all his treasure
That eyeballs are physically heavier than gold
That he should return all his wealth
quiz.e: The Sages explained that the eyeball represents human desire, endlessly unsatisfied while sight remains — a lesson drawn from Proverbs 27:20 about the eyes never being satiated.

quiz.q: According to Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya, how do Torah scholars 'increase peace in the world,' based on Isaiah 54:13?
o: By avoiding conflict entirely
By reading 'your children' (בָּנַיִךְ) as 'your builders' (בּוֹנַיִךְ) — scholars literally build and increase peace through their study
By serving as judges in every dispute
By teaching only in times of war
quiz.e: Rabbi Elazar ben Azarya's teaching plays on the similar Hebrew words for 'children' and 'builders,' suggesting Torah scholars actively construct peace in the world.

quiz.q: According to the new mishna, who was eligible to participate in the third lottery, for burning the incense?
o: Only the High Priest
Only priests who had never before burned the incense — a once-in-a-lifetime honor
Only the most senior priests
Any priest present, regardless of prior experience
quiz.e: The mishna specifies that only new priests — those who had never previously performed the incense service — were called to participate in this particular lottery.
